title: Vayigash: does my father live? (Genesis 45:3)
hook: Joseph's first words after "I am Joseph" are about his father
tomorrow: Vayigash: don't fall out on the way

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vayigash: Judah drew near and offered himself in place of his youngest brother. Your line was draw near. Did you take one step toward a hard conversation? Today, the man he was pleading with breaks. Day two hundred twelve.

Judah has just finished speaking. He's described an old man at home who will die of grief if the youngest son doesn't come back. And the ruler of Egypt can't hold it in anymore. He clears the room: everyone out. The servants go. Now it's only him and his brothers. He cries so loudly the Egyptians hear it through the walls. Then he says two sentences. The first is the line people know. The second one is today.

In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?" In Hebrew it's five words. Ani Yosef, I am Joseph. Ha'od avi chai, is my father still alive? And the brothers can't answer. The text says they were terrified in front of him. Now here's the puzzle the rabbis loved. Joseph already knows the answer. Judah has spent his whole speech talking about their living father. So why ask? One answer: it isn't a question for information. It's the first thing that comes out of a son who hasn't seen his father since the day he was sold. Everything else, the power, the grain, the revenge he could take, falls away, and what's left is: Dad. Is he really alive? Another answer is sharper. Some readers hear a rebuke underneath it. You talk about our father's grief, Judah? Where was that concern the day you sold me? A midrash says that when the brothers couldn't answer this one question, a sage later sighed: if a brother's words left them speechless, how will any of us answer on the day we're asked about our own lives? Both readings can be true at once. And notice what Joseph does next. He says, come near to me, please. The same verb as yesterday. Judah drew near to plead. Now Joseph asks all of them to draw near to be forgiven. The first thing a lost son asks about is the parent. Joseph waited years to ask it out loud. Some people wait longer than they meant to.
screen: `I AM JOSEPH.` · `IS MY FATHER STILL ALIVE?` · `A CRY, OR A REBUKE?` · `COME NEAR TO ME, PLEASE.` · then, large: `DOTH MY FATHER YET LIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: call a parent or an elder. First, the sit. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one older person who shaped you: a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, an old neighbor. Picture their face. Ask yourself Joseph's question in your own words: how are they, really? If they're living, decide when you'll call, today. If they've died, let yourself remember one thing they used to say. The bell holds the time.
Vayigash. The portion where Joseph finally says I am Joseph, and his very next words ask after his father.
Your line: doth my father yet live. Today, call or visit one parent or elder, and ask how they really are. If you can't, say their name aloud once. Day two hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Honoring father and mother is one of the Ten Commandments, and Jewish law spells it out in practical ways: providing for aging parents, standing when they enter, not contradicting them harshly, and saying Kaddish for them after they die.

match.prompt: the two sentences — tap the pairs.

myth: Joseph asked because nobody had told him his father was alive
Judah had just spoken at length about their living father. that's why the rabbis ask why he asked.
Joseph sent everyone else out before revealing himself
he cleared the room, then wept so loudly the Egyptians heard.
some readers hear a rebuke in Joseph's question
where was your concern for our father when you sold me? the brothers had no answer.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. the room is empty except for the brothers who sold you. you've just said I am Joseph. what comes out next?
options: a list of what they did to you.
fork.reveal: Joseph's next words were about his father: is he still alive? the brothers were too shaken to answer.

original.note: Hebrew: is my father still alive? Joseph's words right after I am Joseph (Genesis 45:3).

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph wanted news from home.
what it means: a son's first cry after all those years, and maybe a rebuke, since Judah had just described their father.
what a scholar hears: Genesis Rabbah draws a lesson from the brothers' silence: if they couldn't answer Joseph's rebuke, how will anyone answer God's?

sources.quoted: I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?

notes: The midrash about the brothers' silence and the day of rebuke (attributed to Abba Kohen Bardela) is cited from memory as Genesis Rabbah 93:10; confirm reference and paraphrase.
'Over twenty years' apart: Joseph sold at 17 (37:2), stands before Pharaoh at 30 (41:46), plus seven years of plenty and two of famine (45:6), about 22 years; confirm.
The 'rebuke' reading is one of several commentators' readings; a Keeper may want it attributed to a named commentator.

Editor review (2026-10-01): fixed two factual errors: the hook said 'the eleven brothers who sold him' (Benjamin had no part in the sale, and Reuben was absent), and the teach said the Hebrew is six words (ani Yosef ha'od avi chai is five). Removed the unsourced 'twenty years' figures and the 'most of us' line.
